newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Organized crime sets the tune for Rio's carnival.
newsitem.headline: Organized crime sets the tune for Rio's carnival.

text.p: As Rio de Janeiro prepared to kick off its annual four-day carnival extravaganza beginning on Friday, police on Thursday investigated the city's samba schools for suspected links to drug traffickers.

For decades authorities turned a blind eye to the well-known fact that Brazil's illegal gambling bosses bankroll the world-famous carnival parades, but the presence of the druglords was seen with greater concern.

"Everybody knows about the 'bicheiros' (as the gambling bosses are commonly known)," a police spokesman said. "But, we've also had indications of possible links between drug traffickers and some of the samba schools which has led to an investigation."
Police began asking questions when they arrested a drug trafficker last year who paraded with the Unidos de Vila Isabel samba school.
He admitted the school was pressured by drug traffickers to pick the samba song of their choice for this year's carnival.
Police believed the traffickers wanted to boost their prestige with the shantytown communities where they operate by participating in the popular cultural tradition of carnival.

The schools and their representative body, the Independent League of Samba Schools (LIESA), denied any ties to drug traffickers, and no one questioned the bicheiros' decisive role in the world of carnival.
"What we have today exists thanks to their (the bicheiros') work," said a LIESA spokesman. "Without their backing, carnival wouldn't be as spectacular as it is."
The bicheiros, who run a multi-million dollar illegal lottery known as the "jogo do bicho" (animal game) have ingratiated themselves with the public and the authorities.
They financed the samba schools as well as soccer clubs -- two things dearest to Brazilian hearts. They also have been known to pay kickbacks to police and politicians.
The jogo do bicho is as deeply ingrained in Brazilian culture as carnival itself. Its roots go back to the 19th century when it was introduced as a way of financing Rio de Janeiro's zoo.
Gamblers would bet money on animals instead of numbers and the game quickly became a national pastime and a highly lucrative business despite the ban.

Over the years, however, the bicheiros moved from monkeys and elephants to drugs, arms-smuggling and money-laundering while the animal game became the front for a far more diversified organised crime network.
They control seven of Rio's 16 top-rank samba schools, paying a large chunk of their carnival budgets, which could be between $400,000 and $1.5 million this year, LIESA said.
Their money still makes or breaks Rio's pre-Lent revelry, expected to attract 300,000 foreign and domestic tourists this year.
